But updating our structures can never mean abandoning our principles. It must be applying those principles with even greater determination. The United Nations is not just a platform. It is a promise. So my message to leaders comes down to this: Keep your promises. Live up to the UN Charter. Be true to the ideals you pledged to uphold. Defend international law. Protect human rights. Invest in sustainable and inclusive development. And push for peace, now more than ever. At this crucial moment in the Middle East, de-escalation must be priority one, priority two, and priority three. At the same time, we are well into the fifth year of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with immense civilian suffering, cascading global consequences, and no end in sight. It's time for an immediate ceasefire as a first step towards a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace in line with UN Charter, international law, and relevant UN resolutions. Dear ladies and gentlemen of the media, as we look to threats around the world, let me say a final word about rising concerns regarding the advance of artificial intelligence. AI has enormous potential to accelerate sustainable development, enhance learning, strengthen health systems, boost climate resilience, and so much more. But a growing number of those building it are sounding the alarm. warning that development is racing ahead of our understanding of the risks. Some call for a pause, many call for guardrails. And we cannot afford to ignore concerns that have been raised, especially by those on the front lines of the development of AI. Governments must assume their responsibilities. It is the first responsibility of any government to protect its citizens including from the threats of artificial intelligence. National action is essential, but global coordination is also indispensable because AI does not stop at borders and neither do its risks. Voluntary pauses that are isolated, unverifiable, and unevenly applied will not address the problem. If we believe AI development should slow when risks become too great, We need more than good intentions. Through the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, we have brought together global scientific expertise to ensure that policy is guided by evidence. And artificial intelligence will certainly be a major topic in my discussions with world leaders next week, and the United Nations will continue to explore practical ideas and approaches in the immediate days ahead. We need a shared understanding on how to advance the safe, secure, and responsible development of AI, while identifying when increasingly powerful systems may require stronger safeguards or additional measures to manage potential risks. And this requires genuine international cooperation and a coordinated global effort. I am aware of the geopolitical divides and the temptations they might generate. But the world cannot afford a race to the bottom on AI safety. We need guardrails to build trust and that make AI safe, transparent, accountable, with human dignity at the center. At a time when the world faces three existential threats, runaway artificial intelligence, the climate crisis, and the intolerable deepening of inequalities, international cooperation is more necessary than ever.
